items.title: Identifying Interactions at Scale for LLMs
items.summary: Understanding the behavior of complex machine learning systems, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), is a critical challenge in modern artificial intelligence. Interpretability research aims to make the decision-making process more transparent to model builders and impacted humans, a step toward safer and more trustworthy AI. To gain a comprehensive understanding, we can analyze these systems through different lenses: feature attribution , which isolates the specific input features driving a prediction ( Lundberg & Lee, 2017 ; Ribeiro et al., 2022 ); data attribution , which links model behaviors to influential training examples ( Koh & Liang, 2017 ; Ilyas et al., 2022 ); and mechanistic interpretability , which dissects the functions of internal components ( Conmy et al., 2023 ; Sharkey et al., 2025 ). Across these perspectives, the same fundamental hurdle persists: complexity at scale . Model behavior is rarely the result of isolated components; rather, it emerges from complex dependencies and patterns. To achieve state-of-the-art performance, models synthesize complex feature relationships, find shared patterns from diverse training examples, and process information through highly interconnected internal components. Therefore, grounded or reality-checked interpretability methods must also be able to capture these influential interactions . As the number of features, training data points, and model components grow, the number of potential interactions grows exponentially, making exhaustive analysis computationally infeasible. In this blog post, we describe the fundamental ideas behind SPEX and ProxySPEX , algorithms capable of identifying these critical interactions at scale. Attribution through Ablation Central to our approach is the concept of ablation , measuring influence by observing what changes when a component is removed. Feature Attribution: We mask or remove specific segments of the input prompt and measure the resulting shift in the predictions. Data Attribution: We train models on different subsets of the training set, assessing how the model's output on a test point shifts in the absence of specific training data. Model Component Attribution (Mechanistic Interpretability): We intervene on the model's forward pass by removing the influence of specific internal components, determining which internal structures are responsible for the model's prediction. In each case, the goal is the same: to isolate the drivers of a decision by systematically perturbing the system, in hopes of discovering influential interactions. Since each ablation incurs a significant cost, whether through expensive inference calls or retrainings, we aim to compute attributions with the fewest possible ablations . Masking different parts of the input, we measure the difference between the original and ablated outputs. SPEX and ProxySPEX Framework To discover influential interactions with a tractable number of ablations, we have developed SPEX (Spectral Explainer). This framework draws on signal processing and coding theory to advance interaction discovery to scales orders of magnitude greater than prior methods. SPEX circumvents this by exploiting a key structural observation: while the number of total interactions is prohibitively large, the number of influential interactions is actually quite small. We formalize this through two observations: sparsity (relatively few interactions truly drive the output) and low-degreeness (influential interactions typically involve only a small subset of features). These properties allow us to reframe the difficult search problem into a solvable sparse recovery problem. Drawing on powerful tools from signal processing and coding theory, SPEX uses strategically selected ablations to combine many candidate interactions together. Then, using efficient decoding algorithms, we disentangle these combined signals to isolate the specific interactions responsible for the model's behavior. In a subsequent algorithm, ProxySPEX , we identified another structural property common in complex machine learning models: hierarchy . This means that where a higher-order interaction is important, its lower-order subsets are likely to be important as well. This additional structural observation yields a dramatic improvement in computational cost: it matches the performance of SPEX with around 10x fewer ablations . Collectively, these frameworks enable efficient interaction discovery, unlocking new applications in feature, data, and model component attribution. Feature Attribution Feature attribution techniques assign importance scores to input features based on their influence on the model's output. For example, if an LLM were used to make a medical diagnosis, this approach could identify exactly which symptoms led the model to its conclusion. While attributing importance to individual features can be valuable, the true power of sophisticated models lies in their ability to capture complex relationships between features. The figure below illustrates examples of these influential interactions: from a double negative changing sentiment (left) to the necessary synthesis of multiple documents in a RAG task (right). The figure below illustrates the feature attribution performance of SPEX on a sentiment analysis task. We evaluate performance using faithfulness : a measure of how accurately the recovered attributions can predict the model's output on unseen test ablations. We find that SPEX matches the high faithfulness of existing interaction techniques (Faith-Shap, Faith-Banzhaf) on short inputs, but uniquely retains this performance as the context scales to thousands of features. In contrast, while marginal approaches (LIME, Banzhaf) can also operate at this scale, they exhibit significantly lower faithfulness because they fail to capture the complex interactions driving the model's output. SPEX was also applied to a modified version of the trolley problem, where the moral ambiguity of the problem is removed, making "True" the clear correct answer. Given the modification below, GPT-4o mini answered correctly only 8% of the time. When we applied standard feature attribution (SHAP), it identified individual instances of the word trolley as the primary factors driving the incorrect response. However, replacing trolley with synonyms such as tram or streetcar had little impact on the prediction of the model. SPEX revealed a much richer story, identifying a dominant high-order synergy between the two instances of trolley , as well as the words pulling and lever, a finding that aligns with human intuition about the core components of the dilemma. When these four words were replaced with synonyms, the model's failure rate dropped to near zero. Data Attribution Data attribution identifies which training data points are most responsible for a model's prediction on a new test point. Identifying influential interactions between these data points is key to explaining unexpected model behaviors. Redundant interactions, such as semantic duplicates, often reinforce specific (and possibly incorrect) concepts, while synergistic interactions are essential for defining decision boundaries that no single sample could form alone. To demonstrate this, we applied ProxySPEX to a ResNet model trained on CIFAR-10, identifying the most significant examples of both interaction types for a variety of difficult test points, as shown in the figure below. As illustrated, synergistic interactions (left) often involve semantically distinct classes working together to define a decision boundary. For example, grounding the synergy in human perception, the automobile (bottom left) shares visual traits with the provided training images, including the low-profile chassis of the sports car, the boxy shape of the yellow truck, and the horizontal stripe of the red delivery vehicle. On the other hand, redundant interactions (right) tend to capture visual duplicates that reinforce a specific concept. For instance, the horse prediction (middle right) is heavily influenced by a cluster of dog images with similar silhouettes. This fine-grained analysis allows for the development of new data selection techniques that preserve necessary synergies while safely removing redundancies. Attention Head Attribution (Mechanistic Interpretability) The goal of model component attribution is to identify which internal parts of the model, such as specific layers or attention heads, are most responsible for a particular behavior. Here too, ProxySPEX uncovers the responsible interactions between different parts of the architecture. Understanding these structural dependencies is vital for architectural interventions, such as task-specific attention head pruning. On an MMLU dataset (highschool‐us‐history), we demonstrate that a ProxySPEX-informed pruning strategy not only outperforms competing methods, but can actually improve model performance on the target task . On this task, we also analyzed the interaction structure across the model's depth. We observe that early layers function in a predominantly linear regime, where heads contribute largely independently to the target task. In later layers, the role of interactions between attention heads becomes more pronounced, with most of the contribution coming from interactions among heads in the same layer. What's Next? The SPEX framework represents a significant step forward for interpretability, extending interaction discovery from dozens to thousands of components . We have demonstrated the versatility of the framework across the entire model lifecycle: exploring feature attribution on long-context inputs, identifying synergies and redundancies among training data points, and discovering interactions between internal model components. Moving forwards, many interesting research questions remain around unifying these different perspectives, providing a more holistic understanding of a machine learning system. It is also of great interest to systematically evaluate interaction discovery methods against existing scientific knowledge in fields such as genomics and materials science, serving to both ground model findings and generate new, testable hypotheses. We invite the research community to join us in this effort: the code for both SPEX and ProxySPEX is fully integrated and available within the popular SHAP-IQ repository. https://github.com/mmschlk/shapiq (SHAP-IQ Github) https://openreview.net/forum?id=KI8qan2EA7 (ProxySPEX NeurIPS 2025) https://openreview.net/forum?id=pRlKbAwczl (SPEX ICML 2025) https://openreview.net/forum?id=glGeXu1zG4 (Learning to Understand NeurIPS 2024)

items.title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.

items.title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale
items.summary: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. These limitations lead to load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes and eviction of KV caches that agents will reuse. We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that adapts compute allocation to agent workloads and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We decouple compute allocation from key--value (KV) cache management, allowing nodes to switch efficiently between prefill and decode. Building on this design, an online planner matches the PD split to workload composition, while an agent-aware distributed KV manager guides cache eviction and transfer with signals from agent context management. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, Evolving Infra reduces mean end-to-end request latency and P95 TTFT by up to 4.1x and 14x over Dynamo, NVIDIA's production framework.

items.title: Fuse-All MoE Inference Kernel with Load Balancing on TPUs
items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures activate only a subset of experts for each token, allowing large language models (LLMs) to scale parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation per token. However, intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads limit the efficiency of MoE inference on TPUs. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce Fuse-All MoE, a TPU kernel design that jointly optimizes expert computation, output communication, and load balancing. The kernel fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes, retaining expert computation intermediates on chip. Fixed token-slot destinations allow scheduling and expert placement to change while preserving routing semantics. In prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving, Fuse-All MoE balances EP16 prefill workloads through scheduling and expert redistribution, while symmetric EP8TP2 shares active expert computation between the two TensorCore devices within each chip during decode. Our experiments show that Fuse-All MoE reduces kernel runtime for a measured skewed EP16 prefill workload from 2.3x to 1.09x the same fixed reference time for a balanced workload. Across 32-512 decode tokens, symmetric EP8TP2 reduces kernel latency by up to 21.3% relative to fused EP16. With accompanying serving stack optimizations, the integrated system improves serving throughput by up to 34.5% over the Megablox EP16 baseline.

items.title: Teaching AI to create visuals with more common sense
items.summary: Teaching AI to create visuals with more common sense aconner Mon, 07/01/2019 - 10:07 Article July 01 '19 Adam Conner-Simons, MIT CSAIL An MIT/IBM system could help artists and designers make quick tweaks to visuals while also helping researchers identify "fake" images. Today's smartphones often use artificial intelligence (AI) to help make the photos we take crisper and clearer. But what if these AI tools could be used to create entire scenes from scratch? A team from MIT and IBM has now done exactly that with "GANpaint Studio," a system that can automatically generate realistic photographic images and edit objects inside them. In addition to helping artists and designers make quick adjustments to visuals, the researchers say the work may help computer scientists identify "fake" images. David Bau, a PhD student at MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL), describes the project as one of the first times computer scientists have been able to actually "paint with the neurons" of a neural network — specifically, a popular type of network called a generative adversarial network (GAN). Available online as an interactive demo , GANpaint Studio allows a user to upload an image of their choosing and modify multiple aspects of its appearance, from changing the size of objects to adding completely new items like trees and buildings. Boon for designers Spearheaded by MIT professor Antonio Torralba as part of the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab he directs, the project has vast potential applications. Designers and artists could use it to make quicker tweaks to their visuals. Adapting the system to video clips would enable computer-graphics editors to quickly compose specific arrangements of objects needed for a particular shot. (Imagine, for example, if a director filmed a full scene with actors but forgot to include an object in the background that's important to the plot.) GANpaint Studio could also be used to improve and debug other GANs that are being developed, by analyzing them for "artifact" units that need to be removed. In a world where opaque AI tools have made image manipulation easier than ever, it could help researchers better understand neural networks and their underlying structures. "Right now, machine learning systems are these black boxes that we don't always know how to improve, kind of like those old TV sets that you have to fix by hitting them on the side," says Bau, lead author on a related paper about the system with a team overseen by Torralba. "This research suggests that, while it might be scary to open up the TV and take a look at all the wires, there's going to be a lot of meaningful information in there." One unexpected discovery is that the system actually seems to have learned some simple rules about the relationships between objects. It somehow knows not to put something somewhere it doesn't belong, like a window in the sky, and it also creates different visuals in different contexts. For example, if there are two different buildings in an image and the system is asked to add doors to both, it doesn't simply add identical doors — they may ultimately look quite different from each other. "All drawing apps will follow user instructions, but ours might decide not to draw anything if the user commands to put an object in an impossible location," says Torralba. "It's a drawing tool with a strong personality, and it opens a window that allows us to understand how GANs learn to represent the visual world." GANs are sets of neural networks developed to compete against each other. In this case, one network is a generator focused on creating realistic images, and the second is a discriminator whose goal is to not be fooled by the generator. Every time the discriminator 'catches' the generator, it has to expose the internal reasoning for the decision, which allows the generator to continuously get better. "It's truly mind-blowing to see how this work enables us to directly see that GANs actually learn something that's beginning to look a bit like common sense," says Jaakko Lehtinen, an associate professor at Finland's Aalto University who was not involved in the project. "I see this ability as a crucial steppingstone to having autonomous systems that can actually function in the human world, which is infinite, complex and ever-changing." Stamping out unwanted "fake" images The team's goal has been to give people more control over GAN networks. But they recognize that with increased power comes the potential for abuse, like using such technologies to doctor photos. Co-author Jun-Yan Zhu says that he believes that better understanding GANs — and the kinds of mistakes they make — will help researchers be able to better stamp out fakery. "You need to know your opponent before you can defend against it," says Zhu, a postdoc at CSAIL. "This understanding may potentially help us detect fake images more easily." To develop the system, the team first identified units inside the GAN that correlate with particular types of objects, like trees. It then tested these units individually to see if getting rid of them would cause certain objects to disappear or appear. Importantly, they also identified the units that cause visual errors (artifacts) and worked to remove them to increase the overall quality of the image. "Whenever GANs generate terribly unrealistic images, the cause of these mistakes has previously been a mystery," says co-author Hendrik Strobelt, a research scientist at IBM. "We found that these mistakes are triggered by specific sets of neurons that we can silence to improve the quality of the image." Bau, Strobelt, Torralba and Zhu co-wrote the paper with former CSAIL PhD student Bolei Zhou, postdoctoral associate Jonas Wulff, and undergraduate student William Peebles. They will present it next month at the SIGGRAPH conference in Los Angeles. "This system opens a door into a better understanding of GAN models, and that's going to help us do whatever kind of research we need to do with GANs," says Lehtinen. items.title: SS-HSDP: Efficient and Flexible Sharded Data Parallelism via Runtime-Update Decoupling
items.summary: Sharded data parallelism enables memory-efficient training of large models. While efficient training kernels favor packed, kernel-specific data layouts, optimizers may require variant data structures as optimization units. Existing sharded data-parallel frameworks couple these two choices, limiting runtime efficiency and optimization flexibility. To address this, we present \textbf{\our}, a training framework that separates runtime parameters from update parameters, allowing computation layouts and optimization units to be organized independently. Through shared data views and hierarchical sharding, \our supports this separation while avoiding redundant data movement. This design supports a broad range of optimizers, including matrix-based methods such as Muon, and performance optimizations such as fully zero-copy execution. Experiments on video and language model workloads with MXFP8 training show that \our achieves higher Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) than FSDP2, veScale-FSDP, and Megatron-FSDP. At 128 GPUs, MFU improves by up to 21.7\% over the fastest evaluated baseline, with comparable or lower peak memory usage.

items.title: Control-Flow Profiling for Workload Representativeness
items.summary: Workload characterization in performance engineering often replaces expensive target executions with lower-cost proxies, including reduced datasets, miniapps, and training inputs. Such substitutions require empirical verification that the proxy faithfully exercises the target's dynamic execution behavior. This paper presents an address-keyed control-flow profiling methodology and tool suite designed to evaluate workload representativeness directly from compiled, unmodified binaries. We pair time-ordered basic-block vector (BBV) recurrence analysis with exp-branchprof, an experimental Valgrind tool that captures five orthogonal structural profile families spanning branch direction bias, four-bit global history contexts, dynamic indirect targets, function call transitions, and intraprocedural CFG edges. Our method compares weighted event distributions from two executions of the same binary. It reports support coverage, reference event-mass coverage, distribution distance, entropy-derived quantities, and phase structure, rather than claiming that a single similarity score certifies a proxy. We validate the tool with exact-oracle microbenchmarks across AArch64 and x86-64, covering conditional and inverted exits, calls, returns, direct and indirect jumps, and forked processes. We then apply the workflow to SPEC CPU2017 and CPU2026 train/reference pairs and seven refrate/refspeed pairs. The corpus contains both close matches and cases where a shorter execution reaches much of the same code but misses substantial target, callgraph, CFG, or BBV event mass. The accompanying artifact supports the same analysis for proprietary workload/proxy pairs without requiring raw PC-level profiles to leave the collection environment.

items.title: CHARMING: Parallel Edge AI Acceleration Across Tensor Processing and In-Memory Computation
items.summary: Edge AI increasingly relies on specialized accelerators for low-latency inference under tight resource and energy constraints, yet their efficiency remains limited by data movement. Prior work, CHARM, mitigates this overhead by overlapping data movement with computation. We observe that in-memory computing can further supplement tensor processing as a parallel accelerator while eliminating certain data movements entirely. We present CHARMING, a heterogeneous edge AI architecture that uses accuracy- and quantization-aware partitioning to distribute and concurrently execute inference workloads across tensor processing and in-memory computation. CHARMING partitions attention heads between an AIE array and an in-DRAM compute unit, balancing execution according to model architecture, sequence length, and precision while selecting heads to minimize accuracy degradation. CHARMING also integrates quantization into the AIE projection stage to further reduce data movement. We validate CHARMING end-to-end in hardware on AMD Versal VCK5000 and Alveo U200 platforms and evaluate LLM and video-generation models across multiple precisions using measured hardware results and simulation of the latest in-memory compute hardware. CHARMING improves prefill performance by up to 23.6 percent and decode performance by up to 44 percent over AIE-only acceleration. With int4 x int4 fixed-point in-memory computation, CHARMING reduces per-layer energy by up to 7.6 percent and improves energy-delay product by up to 24.7 percent, while maintaining accuracy similar to a 32-bit floating-point baseline.

items.title: From CUDA to MLX: How K-Search Brings Decades of Kernel Expertise to Apple Silicon
items.summary: Figure 1: CUDA-to-MLX optimization translation map. CUDA optimization knowledge can be translated into architecture-native MLX strategies rather than copied instruction-for-instruction. We face a new epoch in computing. Hardware is changing rapidly — not just faster GPUs, but a growing range of chips from different vendors, each with its own architecture and often tailored to specific AI workloads. Software is changing just as fast, and AI coding tools now generate in minutes what took months of effort a few years ago. With so much of computing now centered on AI, GPU kernels are a crucial component of its success. These are the low-level programs that run inside the GPU, and writing efficient ones is far from obvious — it takes years of expertise to get right. Transferring a kernel from one vendor's hardware to another is harder still, and often means rediscovering the same optimizations from scratch. The CUDA ecosystem, for example, has accumulated decades of hard-won kernel expertise: hand-tuned implementations of attention, state space models, and other critical operations representing thousands of engineering hours. Newer hardware ecosystems (Apple Silicon, custom AI accelerators, and others) are growing fast but lack this depth. In this work we ask whether that expertise can be transferred automatically. We built on K-Search , an evolutionary kernel search framework introduced by Cao et al. at Berkeley Sky Lab that uses AI to optimize GPU kernels, and extended it with a backend for MLX — Apple's machine-learning framework for its own Apple Silicon chips. We developed a novel structured CUDA-to-MLX translation layer that lets K-Search take existing CUDA kernels as a knowledge base and adapt them into high-quality GPU kernels for Apple Silicon, rather than rebuilding from scratch. We show that our approach reaches near-expert level performance on Apple Silicon with 0.97x speedup compared to the native MLX Attention kernel, and up to a 20x prefill speedup over the community mlx-lm implementation on the Mamba SSM kernel; we report the numbers, and how much of the gain comes from the translation layer, in the sections below. Although we focus on MLX kernels for Apple Silicon, the method is not specific to MLX and applies to any ecosystem where CUDA expertise is transferable. Why MLX? Apple's MLX framework has seen remarkable adoption since late 2023. With Apple Silicon in hundreds of millions of MacBooks and Mac Studios, MLX enables local AI inference without cloud costs. The unified memory architecture makes it especially attractive for mid-sized models (7B–70B parameters on M series chips). Yet beneath this momentum lies a significant gap: many performance-critical kernels that the NVIDIA ecosystem takes for granted: paged attention, optimized SSM scan kernels, fused MoE routing are either absent or naive without hardware-specific tuning. MLX runs models correctly but often leaves significant performance on the table. This gap is what motivates the rest of this post. What is K-Search? K-Search is an evolutionary kernel optimization framework originally developed by our first author Shiyi Cao at UC Berkeley Sky Lab. Given a naive kernel and a hardware specification, it runs an iterative optimization loop: an LLM reasons about which optimizations to try next, a code-writing model generates candidate kernels, and those candidates are compiled and benchmarked on real hardware. Measurements feed back into the search, which keeps refining, pursuing promising directions and dropping dead ends until performance converges. Algorithm 1: K-Search via co-evolving world models. The search alternates between selecting the most promising action, instantiating and evaluating code until improvement stagnates, and evolving the world model through insert, update, and prune operations. Adapted from Cao et al. (2026) . Search is grounded by a Spec: a domain-specific document encoding hardware rules, optimization patterns, and mathematical constraints which keeps generated code from hallucinating invalid primitives and ensures candidates will actually compile and run efficiently. In our runs, a single model (Gemini 3.5 Pro Preview) plays both roles: it maintains the reasoning state and writes the kernels. The reasoning half is prompted as a "GPU kernel performance engineer" and asked to work through a fixed analysis before proposing anything: classify the kernel (reduction, scan, attention/softmax, …), rewrite the reference computation in canonical form, map out data layout and access patterns, and hypothesize the likely bottleneck (bandwidth, latency, compute, or synchronization) in each runtime regime. Only then does it emit candidate optimizations, each as a single change implementable in one iteration. We call the persistent reasoning state a world model . Rather than a flat list of things to try, it is a decision (prefix) tree: each root→leaf path composes a full optimization plan, and sibling branches are competing alternatives. Every node is scored — an overall_rating in [0, 10], a confidence in [0, 1], and per-node impacts on memory bandwidth, register pressure, and compute/hardware fit — so the search can rank partial plans and expand the most promising ones. The tree persists and grows across rounds: refining an idea adds a child node rather than overwriting its parent, and if the best score fails to improve for a few rounds (a stagnation window) the search backs off to explore an alternative branch. A single node, as it appears mid-run on the attention kernel, looks like this: { "action" : "Replace the threadgroup-memory softmax reduction with a register-only reduction: each SIMD group owns 8 query rows and reduces across lanes with simd_shuffle_xor, removing a threadgroup_barrier." , "difficulty_1_to_5" : 4 , "impacts" : { "memory_bandwidth" : 8 , "register_pressure" : 4 , // risk: spill if Br > 8 "compute_hw_fit" : 9 // SIMD width 32 ; keep tile 8 x 8 }, "overall_rating_0_to_10" : 8 , "confidence_0_to_1" : 0.7 } Listing 1: Example K-Search world-model node. Each candidate optimization records a concrete action, estimated hardware impacts, an overall priority rating, and the model's confidence. Figure 2: Overview of K-Search. The framework operates on a Search State $S_t$ structured as a search tree. The tree consists of Closed nodes (blue, visited states with attached program like $x_{12}$) and a Frontier of Open nodes (orange, pending hypotheses like $u_{13}$). The workflow iterates through three phases: (1) Action Selection , where the most promising action node is retrieved from the frontier based on world model estimated priority score $V$; (2) Local Refinement , where a stochastic policy $\pi_{\mathrm{code}}$ samples concrete implementations until stagnation; and (3) World Model Update , where the LLM reasons over the trajectory to update the search tree via Insert (adding new actions), Update (adjusting $V$, e.g., $u_{11}$ dropping from 0.9 to 0.6), and Prune (removing less promising nodes like $u_{10}$). The original K-Search paper evaluated this search strategy on CUDA kernels from FlashInfer. Across GQA decode, MLA decode, MLA prefill, and MoE, K-Search improved more consistently than OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve over the same 120-iteration budget. These results establish the search framework we build on here; the remainder of this post asks whether its optimization knowledge can transfer beyond CUDA. Figure 3: Main results from the original K-Search paper. Across three runs, K-Search achieves stronger best-so-far search scores, per-workload kernel performance, and speedup distributions than OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve on four FlashInfer CUDA kernels. Reproduced exactly from Cao et al. (2026) . Building an MLX backend To bring K-Search to Apple Silicon, we first built a native MLX backend. We implemented a full MLX-specific task adapter for K-Search, including: An MLX task backend in k_search/tasks/ handling kernel compilation and execution on Apple Silicon via MLX's Metal/C++ APIs. Updated kernel generator prompts for writing and modifying Metal/MLX kernels. MLX-specific benchmarking integration using mlx.core measurement utilities. Translating CUDA expertise to MLX However, the more interesting challenge was not simply running K-Search on MLX. The key insight is that expert CUDA kernels encode decades of optimization knowledge that is transferable to Apple GPU if you can bridge the conceptual gap. Simply handing an LLM a CUDA kernel and asking it to port it is not enough: without deep hardware context, it produces code that is syntactically valid but architecturally wrong (wrong tile sizes, invalid primitives, mismatched memory assumptions). Our translation layer consists of: Concept mapping tables: A structured glossary of CUDA primitives and their MLX/Metal equivalents with hard constraints. For example: __shared__ maps to Metal threadgroup memory but with a hard 32 KB limit (vs. NVIDIA's 48 KB) warp_reduce maps to MMA (preferred) __syncthreads() becomes threadgroup_barrier(mem_flags::mem_tg) H100's ~3.35 TB/s HBM3 maps to M3 Max's ~400 GB/s unified DRAM a bandwidth difference that reshapes which optimizations are worth pursuing. MLX-specific hints and patterns: Concrete code-level patterns for operations with no direct CUDA equivalent, such as register-based row reductions using simd_shuffle_xor in an 8×8 MMA tile layout, or the "exp2 trick" (replacing $exp(x)$ with $exp_2(x \log_2 e)$) for faster softmax on Apple's fast $exp_2$ hardware instruction. Reusable assertions: Expert kernel behaviors reframed as properties the evolutionary search must preserve, rather than code to copy. Matching expert kernel performance: the Attention kernel We evaluate three configurations of an MLX attention kernel for Apple Silicon: (1) a naive baseline, (2) pure evolution with no additional provided context, and (3) a full context translation layer, which supplies the optimizer with architecture-specific implementation knowledge extracted from high-performance kernels (e.g., FlashAttention-2), letting the evolutionary search reason about implementation strategies rather than starting from a naive kernel. Together, these three configurations let us isolate the exact impact of the translation layer. Figure 4: Performance scaling of the Attention Kernel through stacked optimizations. The "Full Context" configuration successfully discovers and implements advanced strategies like double buffering and loop unrolling, achieving near-expert performance. The jump from 0.26× to 0.97× the speed of Apple's state-of-the-art attention kernel — illustrates how much the translation layer matters. With full context, the evolved kernel independently discovers the key optimizations in FlashAttention 2: threadgroup memory tiling, online softmax, K-transposition for memory access, and the exp2 trick. The last of these replaces every softmax exponential with a base-2 exponential, \[e^x = 2^{x \log_2 e},\] which is exact and lets the kernel use Apple's fast fast::exp2() hardware instruction directly instead of paying for a base conversion at runtime. A 20× faster prefill: the Mamba SSM kernel To evaluate whether K-Search generalizes beyond attention kernels, we applied it to the state-space model (SSM) kernel used by Mamba. Unlike attention, the computational bottleneck is a recurrent state update rather than a softmax, providing a substantially different optimization challenge. We compare the evolved implementation against the community MLX implementation (mlx-lm) and the PyTorch reference implementation (mamba.py) on an M1 Max. Evaluated on mamba-370m f16, M1 Max 64GB: Metric mlx-mamba (ours) mlx-lm (community) mamba.py Decode 152 tok/s 116 tok/s 40 tok/s Prefill L=512 5,751 tok/s 329 tok/s 1,089 tok/s Prefill L=1024 6,010 tok/s 327 tok/s 1,127 tok/s Prefill L=2048 6,612 tok/s 326 tok/s 1,092 tok/s Prefill L=4096 6,743 tok/s 339 tok/s 1,042 tok/s Table 1: Prefill and decode throughput on mamba-370m (f16, M1 Max 64GB). mlx-mamba (ours) reaches ~20× higher prefill throughput than the community mlx-lm baseline, while decode remains comparable. The ~20× prefill speedup over mlx-lm comes down to one difference: mlx-lm does not implement a parallel scan for the SSM. The state recurrence \[h_t = \bar{a}_t h_{t-1} + \bar{b}_t\] looks inherently sequential, but each step can be written as a pair $(\bar{a}_t, \bar{b}_t)$ under the associative combine \[(a_2, b_2) \circ (a_1, b_1) = \left(a_2 a_1,\ a_2 b_1 + b_2\right),\] which reproduces the recurrence exactly. Because the operator is associative, the whole sequence can be evaluated with a parallel (prefix) scan in $O(\log N)$ dependent steps instead of $O(N)$. mlx-lm skips this and processes tokens one at a time, leaving most of Apple Silicon's compute idle; our evolved Metal kernel applies the scan and makes much fuller use of GPU throughput. The gain shows up in prefill, where the full sequence is available to scan in parallel, and not in single-token decode, where there is only one new token per step and no scan to parallelize — which is why the decode row is roughly flat while prefill is ~20×. mamba.py is slow on both prefill and decode because it is a PyTorch reference implementation that falls back to CPU or MPS on Apple Silicon, forgoing the hardware-specific optimizations that MLX's Metal backend makes possible. What's next? On the two kernels we studied, AI-driven evolutionary kernel search grounded in structured cross-platform translation knowledge reached near-expert performance on Apple Silicon without a team of GPU experts starting from scratch. We do not yet know how far this generalizes, but the result is encouraging. For us the main takeaway is that the bottleneck was not the LLM's ability to write Metal code, but the quality of the context and constraints we gave it. Our CUDA translation layer converts existing NVIDIA kernel expertise into actionable guidance for Apple Silicon, and lets K-Search's evolutionary search do the rest. We are actively extending this work in several directions: supporting new architectures, with current efforts focused on developing new kernels for the IBM Spyre AIU and broader hardware targets; adding more kernels such as paged attention and fused MoE routing; and improving integration with the K-Search evolution loop to make translation context even more automatic. We welcome collaboration and feedback from the MLX and broader AI systems communities. If you are working on kernel optimization for non-CUDA hardware, we would love to hear from you. items.title: User-Schedulable Approximations for Quantized Tensor Programs
items.summary: Quantization lets language models run on edge devices, but it sharply increases the number of tensor kernels a library must maintain: every weight format must be paired with every activation format on every instruction set and GPU, with an encoder and a decoder that agree on the stored bytes. In GGML, the tensor library used by llama.cpp, these kernels are written by hand, and only 8 of the 54 weight-activation pairs it runs on our Arm CPU have a tiled matrix-multiplication kernel. We extend Halide's separation of algorithm and schedule to the representation of values. Each approximation is a codec, an encoder paired with a decoder, composed from reusable units: quantizers, integer representations, bit packers and layouts. A new directive, approximate_by, applies a codec to one stage of a program and returns the encoder and decoder as ordinary stages that Halide can schedule, so both decoders fuse into the register tiles of a matrix product. Optional contracts, such as a round-trip law, are checked by property tests; the law exposed an inconsistent block sum in GGML's q8_1. One algorithm and one schedule library generate 347 kernels for 31 of GGML's and KleidiAI's formats on Arm CPUs and Apple GPUs, covering 38 weight-activation pairs for which GGML has no kernel, in 3.7x less code than GGML and KleidiAI. On an Apple M3 Max, our kernels reach at least 95% of the speed of GGML's format-specific kernels in 91.0% of the cases that have one, with a median speedup of 1.13x, and are faster still where GGML falls back to blocked dot products. Counting Apple's BLAS library, which is usually faster for larger f32 products, we still reach that threshold in 86.9% of CPU cases. A port to x86 with Intel's AMX adds 793 lines of code and matches GGML in 83.5% of its cases.

items.title: MoE Pretraining:Parallelism Layout Changes the Model, Not Quality
items.summary: Large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are trained across many machines, and the way the work is split, the parallelism layout, often changes between runs: a job resumes on a different GPU count, a cluster is resized, or an ablation runs on a new setup. In exact arithmetic the layout should not matter, but in real arithmetic it changes the order in which numbers are added, and some MoE rules such as load balancing and expert capacity are often computed per machine. We ask whether the layout changes the trained MoE model. We pretrain the same small MoE language models (25M to 117M parameters, 20M FineWeb-Edu tokens) with the same seed, data and hyperparameters under 9 data-parallel and expert-parallel layouts, in fp32 on CPUs and fp16 on a GPU, and compare each run with the effect of a new random seed. Across 80 runs we find: (1) The layout does not change model quality, but it does change the model: final predictions differ about 80% as much as with a new seed, and over 90% of routing decisions differ. Any layout, a one-bit change to one weight, or a different CPU thread count has the same effect. (2) The cause is the router: decisions that flip are almost exactly those where two experts were nearly tied (AUC 0.97 to 1.00 in the first 16 steps). (3) More, smaller experts create more near-ties (2.7% with 8 experts, 23% with 64) and less reproducible routing (68% vs. 100% of decisions differ), but outputs do not drift further. (4) A dense model of the same active size is far more stable (0.12x the seed level in fp32, 0.58x in fp16), while the MoE reaches about 0.8x at both precisions and twice as fast. (5) When pretraining resumes on a new layout, timing matters: switching at 84% of pretraining barely changes the final model, while switching at 10%, just after warm-up, changes it substantially. We release code, run logs and data.

items.title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
items.summary: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).

items.title: TQIR: Trellis Quantization with Integer Reconstruction for Bandwidth-Efficient Edge LLM Acceleration
items.summary: Autoregressive large language model (LLM) inference is often limited by external-memory bandwidth, while existing ultra-low-bit trellis quantization reconstructs floating-point weights and leaves runtime Hadamard-transform and decoder costs unresolved. This paper presents TQIR, an algorithm--hardware co-design that decouples storage precision ($S$) from decoded-weight ($W$) and activation ($A$) compute precisions, enabling a better accuracy--hardware trade-off. TQIR performs trellis matching with floating-point candidates offline while constraining each candidate to an INT8 or INT4 codeword that can be reproduced exactly for integer GEMM at runtime. To reduce transform cost while preserving the integer weight path, TQIR relocates the reverse Hadamard transform to the activation side and employs an $H_{128}$ Subspace Hadamard Transform, together with a subspace-aligned $128\times2$ trellis tile that preserves the original 256-weight sequence length. The configurable decoder, synthesized in a TSMC 16-nm process, delivers 307.2~Gweights/s in 0.0509~mm$^2$ and achieves 13.93$\times$ and 1.52$\times$ the normalized decoder-area efficiency of Ecco and Codeword Decomposition, respectively. These results show that fixed-rate trellis compression can reduce weight traffic while sustaining an integer-GEMM datapath matched to the evaluated memory and PE rates.

items.title: Parallel Computing Systems for the Optimal Selection of Process Equipment
items.summary: This monograph addresses the optimal selection of equipment for chemical-engineering systems of multiproduct batch plants, a large-scale NP-hard discrete optimization problem in which, for each processing stage, a unit of standard size must be chosen so that the total capital cost of the equipment is minimized while the system remains operable and produces the required products within a given time horizon. We present the mathematical model of system operation and analyze its computational properties. We then develop a sequential branch-and-bound algorithm and its parallel versions for shared-memory systems (OpenMP), distributed-memory clusters (MPI, master-worker), and graphics processing units (CUDA), including recursive and iterative tree traversal, shared-memory optimization, and branch-divergence reduction. To overcome the exponential growth of the run time, we propose a hybrid metaheuristic in which Ant Colony Optimization finds a feasible initial solution and Simulated Annealing improves it, and we implement it on GPUs with thousands of independent threads. Finally, we propose random, constant, and multi-constant approaches to tuning the parameters of the ant colony algorithm based on statistical analysis of many parallel runs, and we study the program on GPUs of three generations and on nodes with several GPUs. Computational experiments on multi-core processors, clusters, and GPUs show that the parallel hybrid algorithm finds solutions within 0.01% of the branch-and-bound optimum in tens of seconds instead of tens of hours.

items.title: GC-MoE on SM120: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with Warp-Level FP8xFP4 Block-Scaled MMA on Consumer Blackwell
items.summary: Expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts decoding is latency bound: each layer serializes a token exchange, a grouped GEMM over routed experts, and a combine, while only a few tokens per rank are in flight. Prior GC-MoE fused these phases into one persistent, Green-Context-partitioned CUDA Graph on Hopper (SM90) and datacenter Blackwell (SM100). This paper rebuilds the operator for SM120 (compute capability 12.0, e.g. RTX PRO 5000) over PCIe. SM120 exposes block-scaled tensor cores only through warp-level mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf8f6f4: no tensor memory, no two-CTA MMA, no cluster multicast. We rebuild the kernel around a swap-AB warp-level block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights in the register A operand and FP8 activations in B, plus SM120-specific mechanisms: scale-byte selection through MMA immediates, a compact-weights path, an adaptive token-tile geometry, an expert-granular streaming dispatch with a batched bulk-pull engine and a 64-bit deduplicating pull cache, full-width BF16 returns drained by resident relay copiers over a position-major arena, and shared experts folded into the compute role. On 8xRTX PRO 5000 over PCIe the operator is 1.522x and 1.387x faster than the FlashInfer CuTe DSL W4A8 MegaMoE and the Cake MegaMoE across 18 decode points (18/18 wins each), and 1.388x faster than Cake with shared experts fused; all 94 numerical cases and 752 per-rank checks pass, at cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.

items.title: Bit-Sparsity Aware Acceleration with Compact CSD Code on Generic Matrix Multiplication
items.summary: The ever-increasing demand for matrix multiplication in artificial intelligence (AI) and generic computing emphasizes the necessity of efficient computing power accommodating both floating-point (FP) and quantized integer (QINT). While state-of-the-art bit-sparsity-aware acceleration techniques have demonstrated impressive performance and efficiency in neural networks through software-driven methods such as pruning and quantization, these approaches are not always feasible in typical generic computing scenarios. In this paper, we propose Bit-Cigma, a hardware-centric architecture that leverages bit-sparsity to accelerate generic matrix multiplication. Bit-Cigma features (1) CCSD encoding, an optimized on-chip sparsification technique based on canonical signed digit (CSD) representation; (2) segmented dot product, a multi-stage exponent matching technique for long FP vectors; and (3) the versatility to efficiently process both FP and QINT data types. CCSD encoding halves the cost of CSD encoding while achieving optimal bit-sparsity, and segmented dot product improves both accuracy and throughput. Bit-Cigma cores are implemented using 65 nm technology at 1 GHz, demonstrating substantial gains in performance and efficiency for both FP and QINT configurations. Compared to state-of-the-art Bitlet, Bit-Cigma achieves 3.2\texttimes{} performance, 6.1\texttimes{} area efficiency, and 15.3\texttimes{} energy efficiency when processing FP32 data while ensuring zero computing error.

items.title: Direction or Magnitude? Learning Scalars over Task-Calibrated Directions
items.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR, which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. The combination of adaptation quality, a compact trainable state, and training efficiency makes SCALAR a promising approach to resource-constrained fine-tuning.

items.title: Agentic Orchestration for SLA-Constrained Network Slicing in Programmable Mobile Data Planes
items.summary: The Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Technical Specification 23.501 (Release 17) defines Maximum Bit Rate (MBR) enforcement at the User Plane Function (UPF) in fifth-generation (5G) networks. Supporting differentiated service-level agreements across the radio access and core networks requires the UPF to enforce MBR limits according to configured slice priorities. During overload, the challenge is to adapt these limits while preserving that differentiation and avoiding oscillations. Building on programmable enforcement and intelligent orchestration, we propose an agentic control loop combining UPF telemetry with locally hosted Large Language Model (LLM) selection from a finite set of admissible rate candidates. Deterministic logic validates each selection and derives Packet Forwarding Control Protocol (PFCP) updates. The evaluated runs show no oscillations or fallbacks and unchanged highest-priority rate limits. These observations establish configuration preservation; delivered per-class QoS protection remains unmeasured.

items.title: Metal Sandbox: Isolated Execution and Command Scheduling for GPU Coding Agents on Apple Silicon
items.summary: On-device inference requires kernels that make effective use of local accelerators. Efficient training and evaluation of models that generate Apple Metal kernels benefit from native macOS tools and concurrent agent sessions. These sessions alternate between model requests, development commands, and GPU execution, leaving GPU capacity idle for much of a rollout. We present Metal Sandbox, infrastructure that combines restricted per-instance file access, native command execution, and command-level scheduling across interconnected Macs. Each agent retains its workspace and private development environment. Parallel commands can run concurrently, while serial commands share one execution slot per node; eligible waiting commands can migrate to available Macs and return results to the original agent. Integration with Harbor supports task execution, automatic verification, and rollout collection through a common workflow. Controlled experiments on four Mac mini M4 nodes achieve $1.68\times$--$2.05\times$ gains in command throughput under concentrated demand. Sixteen static agent traces give an estimated $2.14\times$ sustained-throughput gain for four sessions per node versus one, assuming continuously replenished sessions and unchanged mean durations. Replaying these measured traces under dynamic scheduling reduces mean tool waiting by 18.8% and batch elapsed time by 22.3%, assuming unchanged phase durations. items.title: Read Once, Answer Many: Parallel Prompting for Shared-Context LLM Inference
items.summary: LLM workloads sometimes ask many independent questions about the same long document, as in document QA, data labeling and LLM-based evaluation. Prefix caching removes the redundant prefill shared by these queries, but each decode step still reads the document's key-value (KV) cache once per question, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and scales with the number of questions. We present Parallel Prompting, which decodes P questions as P independent streams of a single request all at once, fixing this issue. In our method, every step reads the shared document once for all P streams, and a stream-id attention mask, evaluated inside the attention kernel, keeps each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question. We implement Parallel Prompting in SGLang by adding about 80 lines to three existing files and a small engine package; the mask needs no dense tensor, and every decode step has a fixed shape that is captured as a CUDA graph. With CodeLlama-7B, 8k-16k-token documents and 64-256 questions per document, Parallel Prompting is 3.7x faster than stock SGLang with its FlashInfer backend on an A100 and 5.9-6.0x faster on an RTX A6000, on two SGLang releases, including the most recent release. Timed on identical inputs, it is faster than stock SGLang in all 144 runs (2 GPUs x 2 releases x 6 workloads x 6 input sets). Code: https://github.com/jlab-nlp/parallel-prompting

items.title: Neural Simulation-Based Inference for Computational Cognitive Models: A Tutorial
items.summary: Computational cognitive modeling is an increasingly essential methodology to elucidate the mechanisms underlying human and animal cognition. By fitting models to empirical data, researchers can perform parameter estimation, model comparison, and model-based neural analyses to assess competing theories, quantify individual differences, and investigate neural representations. Typically, fitting these models relies on likelihood-dependent methods (e.g., Maximum likelihood estimation or hierarchical Bayesian methods). However, for many reasonable cognitive models, computing the likelihood is computationally intractable, in which case these methods become inadequate. This substantially limits the range of theories that researchers can investigate. Simulation-based inference with neural networks (neural SBI) has emerged as a powerful toolkit to overcome this hurdle. By training deep neural networks on datasets generated through model simulations, neural SBI learns the relation between observable data and cognitive models. This approach enables all the applications of standard modeling while bypassing the likelihood computation, without constraints on empirical data size. Despite its successful adoption across diverse scientific fields, neural SBI remains underutilized in cognitive modeling, partly due to a lack of accessible, domain-tailored guidance. This tutorial addresses this gap by providing a clear workflow for applying neural SBI to cognitive models. We also provide practical use cases and recommendations for reducing the computational and simulation burden, facilitating efficient implementation in real-world research settings. By lowering the technical barriers to neural SBI, this tutorial aims to empower cognitive scientists to investigate richer theory spaces and ultimately propel scientific discovery.

items.title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination
items.summary: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.

items.title: Snoopie: A Multi-GPU Communication Profiler and Visualizer
items.summary: With data movement becoming one of the most expensive bottlenecks in computing, the need for profiling tools to analyze communication becomes crucial for effectively scaling multi-GPU applications. While existing profiling tools including first-party software by GPU vendors are robust and excel at capturing compute operations within a single GPU, support for monitoring GPU-GPU data transfers and calls issued by communication libraries is currently inadequate. To fill these gaps, we introduce Snoopie, an instrumentation-based multi-GPU communication profiling tool built on NVBit, capable of tracking peer-to-peer transfers and GPU-centric communication library calls. To increase programmer productivity, Snoopie can attribute data movement to the source code line and the data objects involved. It comes with multiple visualization modes at varying granularities, from a coarse view of the data movement in the system as a whole to specific instructions and addresses. Our case studies demonstrate Snoopie's effectiveness in monitoring data movement, locating performance bugs in applications, and understanding concrete data transfers abstracted beneath communication libraries. The tool is publicly available at https://github.com/ParCoreLab/snoopie.

items.title: uhd-rfsoc: Bringing Off-the-Shelf RFSoC Boards to Unmodified UHD Applications
items.summary: Next-generation wireless research relies on software-defined radios (SDRs) with more channels and larger bandwidth. The USRP family is one of the most widely used SDR platforms, and much of the wireless software ecosystem is built on top of the USRP hardware driver (UHD). However, each USRP model comes with a fixed channel count, bandwidth, and streaming capability. Off-the-shelf radio frequency system-on-chip (RFSoC) boards, on the other hand, integrate up to 16 analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) and 16 digital-to-analog converters (DACs) operating at several gigasamples per second (GS/s), but existing UHD applications cannot directly use them. We present uhd-rfsoc, an open-source FPGA design and host software stack that turns these boards, including the 16-channel ZCU216 and the RFSoC 4x2, into standard UHD devices without modifying UHD. Through standard UHD calls, applications can configure the carrier frequency, channel count, the per-channel I/Q sample rate, and the wire format. uhd-rfsoc combines timestamped, flow-controlled sample transport in the FPGA with data plane development kit (DPDK) packet processing and vectorized sample conversion on x86 and Arm hosts. The built bitstreams for a number of RFSoC board configurations with varying RF data converter rates, channel counts, I/Q sample rates, and wire formats all successfully pass UHD's built-in streaming benchmarks. We further demonstrate compatibility with unmodified GNU Radio flowgraphs, a custom GPU-accelerated transceiver digital signal processing pipeline, as well as the OCUDU and Duranta 5G radio access network stacks using both software and commodity user equipment.

items.title: Smart Model Routing for Order-of-Magnitude LLM Cost Reduction
items.summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) deliver the strongest response quality but carry per-token prices often more than an order of magnitude above those of smaller, task-adequate models. Smart model routing addresses this mismatch by assigning each query to the cheapest model expected to answer it adequately, rather than sending every request to the most capable, most expensive endpoint. This paper develops a formal cost-quality optimization framework for routing -- including a derived optimal threshold-policy structure, a calibration-versus-discrimination distinction, a cascade breakeven condition, and a sensitivity analysis over price ratio and traffic skew -- situates that framework against the principal routing architectures and the signals used to estimate query difficulty, and works through a numerical example showing how a calibrated router can reduce blended inference cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to an always-frontier deployment under specific, stated pricing and traffic assumptions, reporting both the gross reduction from routing policy alone and the net figure with the router's own overhead priced in. We situate this figure against the range reported by published routing systems (roughly 2x to frontier-level accuracy at one-fifth the cost), and close with the practical risks -- under- and over-routing, aggregate quality constraints masking segment-level harm, calibration without discrimination, calibration drift, prompt injection into routing signals, and operational failures such as tier outages and multi-provider price variation -- that determine whether the savings materialize in production. The analysis is primarily analytical, complemented by a GSM8K evaluation of the cascade framework (Section 5), validated (Section 5.2); extending the evaluation across tasks and model families is future work.

items.title: LLMRunner: Closed Workload Model Performance Testing Framework for LLM Servings
items.summary: Performance testing large language model (LLM) serving engines is a crucial requirement considering the criticality of the infrastructure for deploying conversational AI at scale. Most of the benchmarking tools used to carryout performance evaluation of LLM serving do not capture realistic workload orchestration unlike closed workload performance testing infrastructure used in other domains such as web and database engines. For example, state-of-the-art LLM benchmarks for performance testing model traffic as streams of independent single-turn and stand-alone requests omitting the end-user behavior such as think-time between conversational turns. We present LLMRunner, a performance tester for LLM serving that addresses this gap by providing a framework to generate realistic load consisting of multi-turn conversations with configurable end-user parameters such as number of users in the workload loop, think-time distributions etc. Moreover, LLMRunner provides declarative matrix-sweep experiment plans, integrated GPU and KV-cache monitoring, and an automated artifact collection and plotting subsystem. We use LLMRunner to comparatively analyze the performance of LLM serving when NVIDIA CUDA Unified Virtual Memory (UVM) is used as a drop-in replacement memory allocator for the Key-Value cache (KV-Cache). Our test demonstrates that UVM incurs no measurable throughput or latency penalty compared to the baseline memory allocation technique for non-oversubscription scenarios.

items.title: OrbitWeaver: LLM Agent Planning with Simulation Feedback for Optically Interconnected Orbital GPU Clusters
items.summary: Space-based data-center designs increasingly consider GPU computing formations connected by inter-satellite optical links. With limited neighboring connections, jobs assigned disjoint GPUs can still contend on shared relay paths. Rank placement and communication priorities jointly affect this contention and the readiness of downstream computation. We present OrbitWeaver, an offline large language model (LLM) agent planner that jointly optimizes rank placement and communication order. Guided by communication structure, execution dependencies, and simulation feedback, the agent constructs and refines plans that coordinate shared-link access with computation progress. This coordination reduces contention and dependency blocking, shortening mean job completion time (JCT). Simulation experiments on optically interconnected orbital GPU clusters show that OrbitWeaver reduces aggregate mean JCT by 6.2-33.5% relative to the state-of-the-art baselines CASSINI, Crux, and Symphony. These results demonstrate the value of LLM-guided planning for efficient concurrent computing in orbital GPU clusters.

items.title: Mobile Edge Deployment and Resource Management for Maritime Wireless Networks
items.summary: Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) has been envisioned as one of the key technologies for supplying computation and storage resources in Internet of Vessels (IoV) networks. Due to its flexible deployment, low cost and agile maneuverability, Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) has emerged as a promising solution, to provide communication and computation services for maritime users. To this end, we formulate an optimization problem to minimize the expected response time by jointly optimizing the deployment of mobile USVs and computation offloading decisions. To solve the mixed-integer nonlinear program problem, we propose a Dual-Layer Reinforcement Learning (DLRL) framework to attain a near-optimal solution. Specifically, a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm is designed to obtain the best USV deployment in the outer layer learning, and a Q-learning algorithm is designed to determine the best computation offloading decisions in the inner layer learning. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed solution outperforms some literature algorithms by effectively handling both continuous and discrete variables.

items.title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help
items.summary: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

items.title: SIMTurn: Lightweight Divergent Subgroup Scheduling for Intra-Warp Synchronization
items.summary: Stack-based reconvergence enables efficient SIMT execution with a shared warp program counter and compact control-flow state. However, its fixed serialization of divergent paths can deadlock programs that rely on intra-warp synchronization: a spinning subgroup may prevent a resource-holding sibling from executing. Independent Thread Scheduling (ITS) enables finer-grained progress through per-thread execution state, but introduces additional hardware cost. We present SIMTurn, a lightweight compiler-hardware mechanism that enables forward progress among divergent subgroups while retaining stack-based reconvergence. SIMTurn combines a compiler-inserted yield instruction at potentially blocking loops with a bounded pool of resumable subgroups. The scheduler allows a waiting subgroup to yield to a sibling that can make progress, without requiring independent program counters for every thread. We implement SIMTurn in the compiler, simulator, and RTL on the open-source Vortex GPGPU and evaluate it against baseline IPDOM and per-thread ITS schemes. Across the evaluated GPU thread configurations, SIMTurn introduces only 17-24% scheduler-area overhead relative to IPDOM, compared with 39-91% for ITS, and stays within 8% of IPDOM on workloads that never need cross-subgroup progress. On kernels with genuine cross-subgroup parallelism, SIMTurn tracks ITS closely and is up to 2.7x faster than a software-serialized IPDOM baseline.

items.title: A Unified Device-Level Physical Framework for DRAM Read Disturbance
items.summary: Read disturbance in dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) depends on both local device interactions and the electrical conditions imposed by shared array circuitry. Here, we combine DIMM-level characterization results, device measurements, and TCAD simulations to interpret RowHammer, RowPress, and ColumnDisturb within a unified device-level physical framework. We relate charge evolution at the floating storage node to three key mechanisms: trap-assisted electron migration (EM), capacitive coupling (CC), and sense-amplifier-mediated disturb (SAMD). EM is local and trap-sensitive, while CC weakens with wordline separation. SAMD extends disturbance through shared column circuitry by modifying unselected-cell leakage under rail-level bitline biases, a contribution supported by the approximately ninefold higher OFF-state leakage measured relative to retention-like conditions for a high-voltage storage state. These distinct spatial ranges account for localized RowHammer and RowPress failures and remote ColumnDisturb populations with abrupt changes at subarray boundaries. We further interpret prolonged RowPress activation as a transition from an initial RowHammer-like transient to sustained leakage driven mainly by SAMD under held wordline and bitline biases. Within this device-level framework, trap effectiveness and storage-state-dependent leakage provide an interpretation of previously puzzling failure signatures, including the earlier onset of 0-to-1 RowHammer failures despite the predominance of 1-to-0 failures at high hammer counts. The same framework explains the observed RowPress and ColumnDisturb polarities and the duration-dependent reversal of neighboring- and passing-wordline effectiveness. These results provide a physical basis for developing compact DRAM reliability models across access patterns and array configurations.

items.title: Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it. We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate large and variable context lengths. We show how removing the restrictions of the optical ring allows OBM to efficiently serve MoE models. Evaluated at a datacenter scale of 80,000 accelerators, OBM eliminates petabytes of HBM while being competitive or better in throughput and energy per token than an HBM-based system.

items.title: Sparse Matrix Multiplication Exponent 1.5 in the Low-bandwidth Model
items.summary: We study sparse matrix multiplication in the low-bandwidth model: $n$ computers multiply two $n\times n$ matrices, and each computer can send and receive one $O(\log n)$-bit message per round. The input matrices are uniformly sparse, meaning that there are at most $d$ nonzero entries in each row and column, and the task is to compute a uniformly sparse part of their product. In prior work, Gupta et al.~(SPAA 2022) presented an $O(d^{1.907})$-round algorithm over fields for this problem when the sparsity structure is globally known in advance (this is referred to as the supported setting). The upper bound was later improved to $O(d^{1.832})$ rounds. In this work, we give a deterministic algorithm that solves this problem in $O(d^{3/2})$ rounds in the supported setting, improving the previous bounds over fields and semirings.

items.title: Resource Management and Trajectory Optimization for UAV-IRS Assisted Maritime Edge Computing Networks
items.summary: With the exponential growth of maritime wireless devices and the rapid development of maritime applications, traditional maritime communication networks encounter communication and computation limitations in supporting computation-intensive and latency-critical tasks. items.title: INC-SRv6: In-Network Route Exploration and Fast Failover Using Segment Routing Headers in Dynamic UAV Networks
items.summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) networks require a network provisioning mechanism that guarantees delivery and latency quality of service (QoS) under dynamic conditions in next-generation airborne mesh networks by continuously learning and repairing multi-hop paths under rapid link turnover without flooding the control plane.
